interactions.summary: Jiang says the 'lantern of the world' is the sun, identifies it with Apollo, and begins an explicitly interpretive effort to decode the poem's image of four circles and three crosses as the best path for reaching Apollo.
A participant reads the poem's enigmatic line about the path that links four circles with three crosses and tempers the world's wax in its own manner.

Jiang turns the symbolic puzzle into a class exercise: a student guesses the Trinity, Jiang rejects that answer, another student identifies the three crosses with Jesus's crucifixion scene, and Jiang confirms that this is the correct Christian referent.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang explicitly flags the decoding of the four circles and three crosses as his own interpretation rather than settled doctrinal commentary.
Two different students appear to answer Jiang's prompt: one offers the mistaken Trinity guess, and another grounds the three crosses in the crucifixion.

claims.claim: Jiang interprets the poem's 'lantern of the world' as the sun, identifies that sun with Apollo, and says Apollo can reach human beings through different paths.
Jiang says Dante wants to summon Apollo and that the symbolic configuration of four circles with three crosses names the best way of reaching or invoking him.
Jiang presents the decoding of the four circles and three crosses as his own interpretation and invites the class to use imagination rather than rote doctrine to work out the symbol.
Jiang rejects the idea that the three crosses signify the Trinity and instead identifies them with Jesus dying on Mount Calvary alongside two other people.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang openly marks the next move as interpretation and turns symbolic reading into an imaginative exercise rather than a rulebook answer key.
signature_moments.source_phrase: everything that I am saying is my own interpretation
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes the lecture's method explicit and shows that Jiang wants the class to practice interpretive imagination, not just absorb conclusions.

signature_moments.moment: The cryptic geometry of four circles and three crosses becomes the map for how Dante can reach Apollo.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the way that links four circles with three crosses is the best way
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's central symbolic pressure and the hinge into Jiang's larger pagan-Christian paradox reading.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang shuts down the abstract Trinity answer and grounds the three crosses in the bodily scene of Calvary.
signature_moments.source_phrase: when Jesus died, he died on the cross with two other people
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It keeps the symbol concrete and historical, which matters for the paradox he is about to build with the pagan circles.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang glosses this poetic phrase as the sun, identified here with Apollo as the source Dante seeks to reach.
Not the Trinity in Jiang's reading, but the crucifixion scene of Jesus on Mount Calvary with two others.
The unresolved symbolic element Jiang begins to decode through imaginative interpretation as part of the path toward Apollo.

chronology_notes.note: This packet moves from Jiang's Apollo gloss into a staged symbolic exegesis: first establish that Dante is trying to reach Apollo, then anchor the Christian half of the symbol by identifying the three crosses with Calvary.

uncertainty_notes.note: The transcript wording around 'four circles with three crosses' is semantically clear enough for Jiang's lecture, but the exact poetic phrasing may be slightly noisy; preserve Jiang's interpretation rather than over-normalizing the quoted line.
